facts.fact: Resource: Database Internals (Petrov, O'Reilly 2019), ~9h25m, Part I B-trees, page layout, LSM compaction; start here
Resource: DDIA 2nd ed. (Kleppmann and Riccomini, March 2026), ch. 4 Storage and Retrieval ~1h30m, book ~15h
Resource: RUM conjecture paper (Athanassoulis et al., EDBT 2016), ~30 min, six pages
Resource: LSM survey (Luo and Carey, VLDB Journal 2020), 90 min
Resource: Use The Index, Luke (Winand), ~4h: composite ordering, sargability, covering, EXPLAIN
Resource: HNSW paper (Malkov and Yashunin 2016), 45 min

Resource: Colin Scott's interactive latency numbers, ~10 min
RUM conjecture: improving two of read, update, memory overhead makes the third worse
facts.where: R7 (exact quote from the paper), R0

facts.fact: B-trees buy cheap reads with expensive random updates; LSM buys cheap sequential updates with read amplification and compaction; index buys reads with space and write cost; compression buys space with CPU
The question is which corner you give up
facts.where: R0 one idea box, R7 pro box

facts.fact: Write amplification definition: bytes written to device per byte of logical data
B-tree write amp: rewrite 8 KB page for one row, plus WAL, plus full-page writes after checkpoint, easily 10x to 40x
facts.where: R7 correction box and measured table (3.4x appends, about 300x random updates after a checkpoint), R3 (FPI measured)

facts.fact: LSM leveled write amp roughly 10x to 30x at size ratio 10; tiered far less write amp but worse read and space amp
facts.where: R6 (RocksDB tuning guide's worked 33x), R7 measured RocksDB leveled vs universal

facts.fact: Read amplification: B-tree height 3 to 4 page reads plus heap fetch, mostly cached
facts.where: R5 (measured path: 3 index pages + 6 heap pages; depth table)

facts.fact: LSM read amp: one lookup per level, cut by bloom filters (10 bits per key about 1% FP) and in-memory block indexes
facts.where: R6 bloom section (0.82% derived, RocksDB wiki 9.9 bits = 1%), R7 measured blocks per lookup

facts.fact: Space amp: B-tree about 1.3x; LSM leveled about 1.1x; tiered up to 2x or more
facts.where: R7 correction box and measurements (RocksDB space amp; Postgres heap 1.23x of logical; random B-tree fill 66%)

facts.fact: B+ tree: balanced tree of fixed-size pages, updated in place, values in leaves, leaves linked for range scans
Height log_fanout(N); fanout in hundreds; a billion rows 4 levels deep
facts.where: R5 formula, calculator, measured depth to 1e8 (4 levels)

facts.fact: Interior nodes stay hot in buffer pool; point lookup usually one physical read
facts.where: R5 (one or two physical reads), R2

facts.fact: Range scans follow leaf sibling pointers; natural for ORDER BY and BETWEEN
Pain is random writes dirtying pages all over the disk; page split under concurrency needs careful latching
facts.where: R5 (splits, Lehman and Yao, cost box), R3 FPI

facts.fact: Postgres, MySQL InnoDB, SQL Server, SQLite are B-tree engines
Postgres MVCC heap tuples: UPDATE writes a new tuple version and every index must be updated unless HOT
HOT: no indexed column changed and new version fits on the same page
Wide tables with many indexes update slowly; bloat is an operational concern; autovacuum tuning is a production skill
facts.where: R1 cost box, R11; autovacuum tuning owned_by running_postgres_in_production

facts.fact: LSM: memtable + WAL append, sequential writes; flush to immutable SSTable; compaction merges, discards overwritten and deleted keys; reads memtable then files with bloom filters and block indexes
Deletes are tombstones; delete-heavy workloads slow before they speed up; range scans over tombstones are a Cassandra footgun
Compaction strategy is the real knob: leveled low space and read amp, high write amp, RocksDB default and Cassandra LCS; tiered low write amp, worse read and space, for write-heavy ingestion
facts.status: verified (RocksDB options.h, Cassandra docs); note STCS is Cassandra's default

facts.fact: Compaction competes with foreground traffic; falls behind, read latency degrades and disk fills: a metastable failure to alert on
facts.where: R6 cost box (write stalls wiki), Rpro RocksDB row, Rmist

facts.fact: Choosing: B-tree for transactional mixed reads and updates with predictable latency; LSM for write-heavy ingestion, compression, flash write budgets
facts.where: R5 and R6 cost boxes (when not to use), R7 pro box

facts.fact: Analytical column stores are LSM-shaped; ClickHouse MergeTree
A write is not durable until it reaches stable storage, 10,000 times slower than memory
Buffer pool and page cache: Postgres modest shared_buffers plus OS page cache
facts.where: R2 (128 MB default, 25%, 40% quote, effective_cache_size 4 GB)

facts.fact: MySQL InnoDB large buffer pool, mostly bypasses OS cache
facts.where: R2 (80% guidance, O_DIRECT default on Linux since 8.4)
facts.status: verified with correction (O_DIRECT default only since 8.4)

facts.fact: ClickHouse leans on the page cache
facts.where: dropped: not checked; ClickHouse caching owned_by analytics_columnar_and_lakehouse

facts.fact: Cache hit ratio is the most predictive number for OLTP latency; working set exceeding RAM changes p99 character
facts.where: R2 cost box (blks_hit vs blks_read), Rmist

facts.fact: write() moves bytes into page cache; fsync forces them to the device
fsync tens of microseconds on enterprise SSD with PLP; a millisecond or more on consumer or network storage
facts.status: verified/corrected (1.6 to 12 us PLP; 0.9 to 3 ms consumer; 0.74 ms network)

facts.fact: A commit costs at least one fsync; single-row commit rate bounded by fsync latency; group commit batches
synchronous_commit = off buys throughput, loses a small window of commits on crash
facts.where: R3 (measured 7,504/s and 71,439/s; 3 x wal_writer_delay; no inconsistency), Rpro

facts.fact: fsyncgate; Postgres now panics on fsync failure instead of retrying
facts.where: R3 'When fsync fails' (LWN 2018; Feb 2019 minor releases; data_sync_retry)

facts.fact: WAL: append intended change to sequential log and fsync before touching data pages; recovery replays from last checkpoint
WAL turns random durable writes into sequential ones
WAL also drives replication, PITR, CDC (Debezium)
facts.where: R3 last paragraph; owned_by running_postgres_in_production and queues_streams_and_async_work

facts.fact: Checkpoints flush dirty pages so log can be trimmed; periodic IO spikes; checkpoint tuning smooths tail latency
Redo log, journal, oplog, binlog, commitlog: same idea
Index B-tree: equality, range, prefix, sorting, covering index-only scans; default
Composite index: equality columns first, then range; usable up to first range predicate
facts.where: R10 multicolumn (docs and Use The Index, Luke), Rmist

facts.fact: Hash: equality only, slightly smaller and faster; rarely worth it in Postgres; also hash joins and aggregates
facts.where: R9 table and measured hash vs B-tree (hash 3.6x larger here because of B-tree dedup); hash joins owned_by query_planning_and_performance
facts.status: corrected: 'slightly smaller' does not hold against a deduplicated B-tree

facts.fact: GIN: element to list of rows; full-text, JSONB containment, array membership; fast search slow update; pending list
GiST and SP-GiST: framework for data with no total order; geometry, ranges, PostGIS, exclusion constraints
GiST historically the ANN index in early pgvector
facts.status: corrected: pgvector started with IVFFlat (0.1.0, 2021-04-20), HNSW 0.5.0 (2023-08-28), never GiST

facts.fact: Inverted index (Lucene): term to posting list, frequencies, positions, BM25, phrase queries; immutable segments merged (LSM logic)
Bitmap index: one bitmap per distinct value, AND/OR; Postgres builds bitmaps on the fly for bitmap heap scans; combining two mediocre indexes
Skipping and zone maps: min/max per block; ClickHouse sparse primary key, Parquet row-group stats, Snowflake micro-partitions; sort order at write time matters more than indexes
facts.where: R12 (MergeTree 8192-row granules cited), R9 BRIN; Parquet and Snowflake detail owned_by analytics_columnar_and_lakehouse

facts.fact: ANN section: exact search is brute force; recall at k; quote latency with recall
Flat search: exact, baseline, correct below about 100k vectors
HNSW: layers, greedy descent, default in many stores, RAM cost (M x 8 to 12 bytes, 6 KB per 1536-d vector), slow build, soft deletes, knobs M, ef_construction, ef_search
IVF: k-means lists, nprobe, boundary problem, drift, needs training
IVF-PQ: product quantisation 16x to 64x, rerank; FAISS billion-scale; int8 4x, binary 32x
DiskANN (Vamana): graph on SSD; Azure, Milvus disk index, pgvectorscale
ScaNN: anisotropic vector quantisation; Postgres via competitor extensions; Vertex AI
Filtered vector search: pre-filter vs post-filter vs in-traversal; per-tenant indexes; evaluate on this
Planner section: access paths, join algorithms, costing; six failure modes; EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) habit; learned planner 1.81x
facts.status: handed on verbatim with corrections (learned planner corrected; random_page_cost 1.1 folklore)

Latency: read 1 MB from memory 50 us
Latency: NVMe random 4 KB read 50 to 100 us
Latency: fsync enterprise SSD 0.1 to 1 ms
Latency: read 1 MB sequentially from NVMe 200 to 500 us
Latency: same-datacentre round trip 0.5 to 1 ms; cross-region 50 to 150 ms; S3 first byte 20 to 100 ms

facts.fact: Latency: Redis GET 0.2 to 1 ms
facts.where: Rnum 'moved' note (corrected to 0.143 ms loopback vendor figure); owned_by caching

facts.fact: Latency: Postgres indexed single-row read warm 0.5 to 2 ms; 50 ms means N+1 or missing index
Latency: HNSW 1M vectors 1 to 5 ms; retrieval is not the RAG bottleneck
Latency: LLM time to first token 200 ms to 2 s
Habit: multiply operations by cost of one and compare with measured latency; gap is an uncounted round trip or a cold cache
